rationale: B wins because it saw the story hiding in the missing number: "REI won't say how much of its business is used gear." A is cleaner, but it leaves that as homework: "the share of sales that comes from used gear...stays unproven." That is the difference between a pitch list and a reporter's notebook. B still needs its knuckles rapped for "repair benches arrive," because the facts do not say benches.
gaps_in_A: "competitors get benchmarked against" adds an unsupported competitive comparison; the update gives no competitor landscape or benchmark data.
"REI's record member dividend, explained" is viable, but thin until REI gives the actual dividend amount and prior record; A knows this but still spends a whole angle on an empty number.
"the share of sales that comes from used gear...stays unproven" is treated only as missing proof. That nondisclosure is itself a sharper accountability angle.
gaps_in_B: "Trade-in counters and repair benches arrive at REI stores" overstates the facts. The update says members can get repairs at stores, not that benches exist in every location.
"every store needs intake space, grading standards, technicians, and inventory handling" turns unknown implementation details into assertions. Staffing model belongs in proof, not the setup.
"a public retailer answering to shareholders has a hard time cheering on resale, which cannibalizes new-product margin" is plausible but not grounded in the supplied update.
"pushing customers to buy used" is a half-step too far. The facts support resale and trade-in availability, not a stated customer-behavior push.
